sentences.text: For the first trial, Fern picked evening primrose — the real kind, not Grandpa's little pink one.
She and Grandpa planted three of them in the small experimental bed near the greenhouse.
Grandpa had a whole small bed for testing flowers, so you did not have to commit to putting something in the clock until you knew it worked.
The evening primroses grew fast.
By the end of the second week they had buds.
The first flower opened at 7:32 in the evening.
Fern was there with her watch.
She wrote it down.
The second flower opened at 7:40.
The third opened at 7:15.
She showed Grandpa.
"They are all in that range," she said.
"Not five.
More like seven-thirty." Grandpa nodded.
"Beautiful flowers," he said.
"But not for our clock.
Some flowers are stubborn about their hour, and some are flexible, and the ones we want are stubborn.
Try again."
For the second trial, she chose night phlox.
It had white flowers with a strong sweet smell, and the book had said it opened in the late afternoon.
Grandpa was doubtful — he thought it opened too late.
But he agreed to try.
They planted five of them.
They grew.
They bloomed.
They opened at six-thirty in the evening.
Not five.
"Two down," Grandpa said cheerfully.
He did not seem discouraged.
He had done this many times before.
"Third time may or may not be the charm.
Do not worry about it." Fern was worried about it, though.
She was worried the summer was going to end and she was not going to find a good flower and Grandpa would have to wait another whole year.
She started reading more carefully.
She started asking Grandpa questions.
"Grandpa," she said one evening.
"When you chose the flowers for the other hours — did you always know what you wanted.
Or did you have to try lots of things." Grandpa smiled.
"I tried lots of things," he said.
"For nine o'clock in the morning, I tried four different flowers before I found the field marigold.
For noon, I tried maybe six.
Some of the flowers I planted here failed for reasons that had nothing to do with the time.
Some of them just did not like our soil.
Or the deer ate them.
Or a spring frost got them."
"So you have been failing at this for a long time," Fern said.
Grandpa laughed.
"Yes," he said.
"I have been failing at this for a long time.
But every failure — I learn something.
Every time a flower does not open at the right hour, I know a new thing about that flower.
That is not really failing.
It is a way of learning that is slow and honest." He looked at her.
"You are eleven flowers ahead already, Fern.
You do not have to find the twelfth this summer.
You can find it next summer.
Or the summer after.
It does not have to happen fast."
But Fern still wanted to try.
In the fifth week she was walking along the old stone wall at the very back of the garden, where things grew wild that Grandpa had never planted.
And she noticed a small ordinary-looking plant growing in a crack between two stones.
It had thin dark stems and small round green leaves and a few pale buds.
She had never noticed it before.
She sat down and looked at it for a while.
That afternoon she asked Grandpa about it.
She described it.
He said, "Oh, that is just — I think that is a small Scottish thing that grows wild here.
Nothing special.
My mother used to know its name.
I don't remember it.
It has been growing there since before I bought the garden." "Does it flower?" said Fern.
"I think so.
Small flowers.
Nothing showy.
Why?" Fern shrugged.
She said, "I don't know.
It just — feels different." Grandpa raised an eyebrow but he did not tell her to stop paying attention to it.
He said, "Go and watch it.
See what it does.
Never a bad thing to notice a plant."
So Fern went and sat by the wall the next afternoon at four o'clock, with a small alarm clock and a notebook.
She watched.
The flowers were closed.
She read her book.
She looked up sometimes.
At exactly five minutes past five, she noticed something.
One of the small pale buds was starting to open.
It moved slowly — over the next fifteen minutes it opened into a small five-petaled flower, pale lilac in color, with a small yellow center.
By five-thirty it was fully open.
She waited longer.
It stayed open for maybe two hours.
Then, as the light went, it slowly closed again.
She wrote it all down.
She went back the next day.
Same thing.
Opened at five past five.
Closed by seven-thirty.
Same the day after.
She counted for a whole week.
The plant opened at five o'clock every single day, plus or minus five minutes.
She showed Grandpa her notes on Sunday morning.
